# What next for gain-of-function research in Europe?

## Authors

- Robin Fears<sup>1</sup> †
- Volker ter Meulen<sup>2</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. European Academies Science Advisory Council Halle Germany
2. German National Academy of Sciences Leopoldina Halle Germany

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

A working group on gain-of-function research set up by the European Academies Science Advisory Council (EASAC) has emphasised the importance of ensuring that the necessary safeguards and policies are in place

## Scientific responsibility and benefit-risk assessment

Self-regulation is a necessary first step for gain-of-function research, but this does not mean that each researcher is free to decide for themselves what procedures to follow. Everyone involved must conform to existing regulations, codes of conduct and established methods for biorisk management (see EASAC, 2015 for a list of existing regulations in Europe, and details of work by the World Health Organisation and the OECD in this area).

Moreover, proposals for gain-of-function studies—particularly those that intend to alter virus transmission, host range, drug resistance, infectivity, immunity and virulence—have to be justified by their authors to a wide range of bodies (the institutions where the work will be carried out, the agencies that will fund the work, the relevant ethics committees, and the relevant national authorities), as well as their peers, on a case-by-case basis. This process must involve a thorough analysis of the risks and benefits of the research being proposed. Researchers also need to demonstrate that the information they need can only be obtained from gain-of-function experiments.

There are many uncertainties in the data used to evaluate benefit and risk, and this can lead to controversy. It should also be acknowledged that potential benefits of research are sometimes overstated by scientists: however, it is also true that the benefits of research might only become clear much later. Views vary on whether benefit should be quantified in terms of future public health impact or described in terms of the generation of knowledge, and on the extent to which benefits may be lost if research is not allowed. There have been concerns that research that could help to streamline the production of vaccines might suffer if gain-of-function experiments are banned (Cohen, 2015; Ping et al., 2015). Because of the multiple challenges involved in assessing risk and benefit, the EASAC report concludes that any benefit-risk analysis cannot be regarded as a ‘once and for all’ calculation, and that all the relevant parties need to understand and communicate the issues on an on-going basis.

The EASAC report also recommends that there is no need for a new advisory body at the EU level. Rather, all EU Member States should have a clear national advisory mechanism on procedures for assessing and managing biosafety and biosecurity risks. In the UK, for example, the Health and Safety Executive has statutory powers, but other EU Member States have different mechanisms and not all have statutory powers. There is need to harmonise the implementation of good practice in these respects. All countries should also adopt a ‘layered’ approach with researchers, research institutions, research funders and national authorities all being responsible for the regulation of gain-of-function research. Such a layered approach at the country level will spread good practice, increase accountability, and help to improve public trust in research.

Researchers and institutions also have to recognise their responsibility to make decisions about publishing sensitive information and, together with funders, ethics committees and others, need to consider these issues throughout the research process, starting when the research is first proposed, rather than delaying the decision until a manuscript is ready for submission to a journal. The oversight within the scientific community must involve journals and professional societies, as well as researchers, their funders and institutions (and national advisory bodies in complex cases). Journal editors in the US recently came to a similar conclusion (Casadevall et al., 2015). Regarding the question of what to do when European researchers submit a manuscript to a journal that is not based in Europe, EASAC advises that the use of the EU’s export control regime is an inappropriate and ineffective vehicle to block such submissions.

Many of EASAC’s recommendations have been welcomed by the European Commission, who will now consider how to incorporate EASAC advice into guidance for Horizon 2020 research grant applicants and evaluators.

The EASAC report resonates with the themes that are emerging from discussions in the US involving the National Academies, the National Science Advisory Board for Biosecurity (NSABB) and the National Institutes of Health. A National Academies workshop in December 2014 observed that the challenges involved in regulating gain-of-function research were international, that attention should be focussed on those experiments of greatest concern, that researchers and their institutions must accept responsibility, and that analysing the risks and benefits is not straightforward. Since then, a quantitative risk-benefit analysis has been initiated (Casagrande et al., 2015), and the NSABB has set up a working group to look into the issues surrounding gain-of-function research (Kanabrocki, 2015). In its interim report the NASBB working group noted that the US already has a robust policy framework for the regulation of research, and any future policies should build on this framework.

## Challenges for wider engagement

A clear theme in both Europe and the US is the need for the scientific community to engage more broadly with the public, explaining the reasons for doing gain-of-function research, discussing the potential risks and benefits of this research, and explaining the biorisk management practices adopted. Engagement with public interests can be considered at three levels. First, on the global scale, the scientific community has to ensure that the public health benefits that arise from innovation based on gain-of-function research are made available to everyone. Second, on the national level, scientists need to convince the public that taxpayer funds are being spent wisely. Third, on a local level, scientists must engage with those who live near research facilities to reassure them about safety.

Another clear theme is the need for the regulatory authorities, funding bodies and professional societies in different countries to work together to share expertise in the regulation of gain-of-function research and in risk-benefit analysis. Academies of science have a clear role to play at the national level, and international networks of academies can bring scientists from different countries together to study and make recommendations on specific issues: the working group on biosecurity set up by the InterAcademy Partnership is an example of this.

Influenza pandemics are currently unpredictable. However, we still need to be ready for the next pandemic, and that includes being in a position to perform gain-of-function research if that is the only way to obtain the information needed to deal with the pandemic. And, as should be clear from above, this means that many different stakeholders—scientists, institutions, funding agencies, ethics committees, national regulatory authorities, scientific societies and journals—need to work together to ensure that we are prepared.

results.result: EASAC established a working group on gain-of-function research that emphasized the importance of ensuring necessary safeguards and policies are in place.
results.evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are directly stated in the manuscript abstract and represent factual information about the EASAC working group's establishment and its emphasis on safeguards. These are straightforward descriptive claims about the report's existence and main message.

results.result: Self-regulation is necessary but constrained for gain-of-function research, requiring all involved parties to conform to existing regulations, codes of conduct, and established biorisk management methods documented in EASAC 2015 and by WHO/OECD.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 establish a clear regulatory framework where self-regulation exists within defined boundaries. The claims are internally consistent and reference existing regulatory documentation (EASAC 2015). The position that self-regulation does not mean individual autonomy is clearly articulated.

results.result: Gain-of-function research proposals, particularly those altering virus transmission, host range, drug resistance, infectivity, immunity and virulence, must be justified on a case-by-case basis to multiple oversight bodies through thorough risk-benefit analysis, demonstrating that information can only be obtained through such experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 describe a comprehensive justification process with specific requirements. The claims are consistent with each other and establish clear procedural expectations. The requirement for demonstrating necessity (C11) is a logical extension of the justification process.

results.result: Benefit-risk evaluation for gain-of-function research faces multiple challenges including data uncertainties leading to controversy, potential overstatement of benefits by scientists, delayed benefit realization, varying views on benefit quantification, and concerns about impacts on vaccine research if experiments are banned.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 collectively describe the complexities and challenges in benefit-risk assessment. C18 is supported by citations (Cohen 2015; Ping et al. 2015). The claims acknowledge both sides of debates and present a balanced view of assessment difficulties, though they remain descriptive rather than providing solutions.

results.result: The EASAC report concludes that benefit-risk analysis for gain-of-function research cannot be a one-time calculation and requires ongoing understanding and communication among all relevant parties.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 present a clear conclusion from the EASAC report about the dynamic nature of benefit-risk analysis. This is a direct statement of the report's findings and represents a key recommendation for ongoing engagement rather than static assessment.

results.result: EASAC recommends against creating a new EU-level advisory body, instead advocating that all EU Member States establish clear national advisory mechanisms for biosafety and biosecurity risk assessment, noting current variation in mechanisms and statutory powers across Member States (e.g., UK's Health and Safety Executive) and the need for harmonization.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 present a coherent policy recommendation with supporting context about current state variation. The UK example (C23) provides concrete illustration. The recommendation for harmonization (C26) logically follows from the identified variation (C24-C25). These are policy positions rather than empirical findings.

results.result: EASAC recommends a 'layered' regulatory approach involving researchers, institutions, funders, and national authorities, which is expected to spread good practice, increase accountability, and improve public trust in research.
results.evaluation: Claim C27 presents a clear recommendation, but C28-C30 make predictive claims about outcomes (spreading good practice, increasing accountability, improving public trust) without empirical evidence. These are speculative benefits rather than demonstrated outcomes, as indicated by their 'SPECULATION' evidence type.

results.result: Researchers and institutions must recognize responsibility for publication decisions about sensitive information, considering these issues throughout the research process from initial proposal rather than at manuscript submission. Oversight should involve journals, professional societies, researchers, funders, institutions, and national advisory bodies in complex cases. EASAC advises against using EU export controls to block submissions to non-European journals.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C37 present a coherent framework for publication oversight and timing. C36 provides external validation through citation to US journal editors reaching similar conclusions. C37 addresses a specific policy question with clear guidance. The claims are internally consistent and represent practical policy recommendations.

results.result: The European Commission welcomed many of EASAC's recommendations and will consider incorporating EASAC advice into Horizon 2020 guidance for research grant applicants and evaluators.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 describe the European Commission's response to the EASAC report. These are factual statements about institutional reception and planned actions. The claims indicate policy impact but do not guarantee implementation.

results.result: The EASAC report aligns with US discussions involving National Academies, NSABB, and NIH. A December 2014 National Academies workshop identified international challenges, need for focused attention on high-concern experiments, researcher/institutional responsibility, and complexity of risk-benefit analysis. Subsequently, quantitative risk-benefit analysis was initiated and NSABB established a working group, which noted the US has a robust existing policy framework that future policies should build upon.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48 describe parallel developments in the US with appropriate citations (Casagrande et al. 2015; Kanabrocki 2015). The claims establish international convergence on key themes and document specific institutional responses. The progression from workshop observations to subsequent actions is logically presented.

results.result: A clear theme in both Europe and the US is the need for broader public engagement by the scientific community about gain-of-function research, including explaining rationales, discussing risks/benefits, and explaining biorisk management. Engagement should occur at three levels: global (ensuring universal access to public health benefits), national (demonstrating wise use of taxpayer funds), and local (reassuring communities near research facilities about safety).
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C56 present a comprehensive framework for public engagement organized into three clear levels with specific responsibilities at each level. The claims are internally consistent and represent a coherent communication strategy. However, these are normative recommendations about what should happen rather than empirical findings about what has happened.

results.result: International collaboration is needed among regulatory authorities, funding bodies, and professional societies to share expertise in gain-of-function research regulation and risk-benefit analysis. Academies of science have a clear national role, and international academy networks can facilitate cross-country collaboration, exemplified by the InterAcademy Partnership's biosecurity working group.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 describe the role of scientific academies in facilitating international cooperation with a concrete example (InterAcademy Partnership). The claims are consistent and provide both general principles and specific illustrations of the proposed collaborative framework.

results.result: Despite the unpredictability of influenza pandemics, preparedness requires maintaining capability to perform gain-of-function research when it is the only way to obtain necessary information. This requires collaboration among multiple stakeholders including scientists, institutions, funding agencies, ethics committees, national regulatory authorities, scientific societies, and journals.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 present a rationale for maintaining gain-of-function research capability linked to pandemic preparedness. C61 states a factual premise about pandemic unpredictability. C62-C65 build a logical argument for preparedness requiring multi-stakeholder collaboration. The claims are internally consistent and represent a concluding synthesis of the manuscript's themes.
